So all your.
Okay, perfect.
Good morning.
Sorry I'm a couple of minutes late.
Good morning, Richard.
Yeah, two minutes.
Nice to meet you, Andrew.
Two minutes was nothing, was it?

Nice to meet you too, Richard.
Nice to meet you.
Yeah.
So I've given Andy bit of update.
Richard is chair of CoverDee and QueryClick and we're looking at options just seeing what the possibilities are.

Interested to get your view on.

Can I capture that, Richard?

My concern is more around do we actually see any value for this business?
I mean it's.
Is it too small?
Effectively?

But how do we.
Is.
Is there a way of capturing value for that business or is it just at a scale where no one's that interested?
It's too much like hard work for a small business like that.
Yeah, Interesting question.
A lot of people have that idea about M and A funnily enough they think, you know, unless it's a huge play that it's not really worth less.
That more specific to the marketplace.
Right.
I mean I've sold lots of businesses with a million pounds of revenue with a services business where you're kicking off minimal amounts of profit.
So it's 60% margin are you saying at the moment?
Yeah, yeah.
I mean so it's got really good ebitda.
Obviously I'd have to have a sort of deeper look as to why the margin is so big.
I would say that's potentially a slight risk factor, that it's got a huge margin because it usually means that there are no people in sort of positions of responsibility.
You know, it's either a lot of freelancers and just one or two people running the business on their own.
So I guess the main.
So leave your concerns there.
It's all full time employees.
It's full time.
The main thing around service businesses is obviously you're buying the team.

So if you've got a team that's able to generate, you know, 1.2 million revenue with a 6% margin, then I would say that that is definitely something that somebody's going to be interested in acquiring.
What we do tend to find actually is there's a lot more buyers sort of at the bottom end of the market.
So the interesting thing is when you've got a really profitable small business like that, potentially there'll be a lot of interest.
So I think in terms of purely the metrics, there should be a lot of buyers there.
I guess the other aspects to it are the type of business that it is and maybe location and whether it's relocatable.
But you know, performance marketing tends to be really attractive.
You know, a lot of companies want to buy it and it's a nice little bolt on for a lot of marketing businesses.
They can, they're generally looking for that sort of thing to bolt on.
So we get a lot of queries around performance marketing as well.
Are those queries because everybody knows it's a difficult market and they're trying to pick up bargains or are companies that are selling able to generate decent valuations?
Because clearly not just in this sector, but in other sectors, the market is tough.
And so if it's just a case of vultures swooping in to try and get the add ons at low values, then that's.
That's not quite so interesting.
Right?
Yeah, I would say it's probably quite pessimistic look at the market in terms of the way we see it.
You know, most buyers are obviously looking to get the right price.
They have to get the financing in place.
And at the bottom end of the market you're looking at sort of 3x multiples.
But the sort of normal range for an agency, particularly one that's performing quite well, would be somewhere between 4 to 6 and then maybe even.
Sorry, talking about on EBITDA.
Sorry, I missed that last word.
Is the multiple on EBITDA that you're talking about?
Yes, it is, yes.
Yeah.
So I mean software Businesses are priced very differently.
But our EBITDA multiples.
Yeah.
So somewhere between four and six like the usual range for marketing agencies and that can be much higher than that.

It really does depend on a load of other factors like you know, types of clients that you've got, whether there's a lot of client concentration in the, in the mix, you know, whether you've got long contracts, etc.
Etc.
There's a bunch of other things that will push those multiples up.
But yeah, we would have to have a look at that a bit more closely.
But I would say, you know, let's just say generally speaking you're probably looking at a four or five times multiple for a business that size in marketing with really strong ebitda.
I mean that, that looks like.
What would it be at least sort of.
Well, let's say it's four and a half times multiple.
So 3.2 million somewhere around, around there.
Yeah.
I mean there's, there's, that's gross margin.
Right.
So there's probably more cost to come out before the bottom line.
But yeah, so, so what was your ebitda?
I thought you.
Well see this is because we're, we're combined business, we don't have them split out.
So.
Okay.
Because we've got the software cost in there as well.
So we need to, there's a, that, that work has been done before but I don't, I don't have an up to date position on that.
Okay.
So you need to extract it.
So it does, it doesn't have its own balance sheet.
The, the, the business would, we'd need to do some preparation work.
Yeah.
So, but a lot of that prep.
So I've been, I've been pushing for this for quite some time.
So all that work was done about, I think it's about 18 months ago.
Okay.
So.
So it would just be a case of repopulating those models so it wouldn't take long.
And so in the last 612 months, Andy, what, what have you seen?
You know, you seeing those four to six multiples?
We've got some examples of, of what you've seen happen.
So yeah, the last six months.
So we work on the buy and the sell side.
So we see a lot of deals going in both directions.
I mean I would just say 4 to 6 is kind of the typical range.
Actually our own personal experience, we've seen much higher on the sell side as well.
We sold an agency for 13.5 times multiple and we've just bought both an agency in the UK and the US for one client and we paid seven and a half for one and about six and a half for the other.
The one in the UK was, was the cheaper one.
So uplift, certainly the 13 and a half.
What was it that made the difference then?
So they had, they had a platform that you could log into.
It was like a self service platform.
It kind of had, it wasn't really a SaaS business, it was kind of a client portal that sat in front of the agency.
But it did drive value because it had its own revenue in that sort of client portal alongside the agency.
So that did push the multiple up.
So I would say the agency business itself probably was, I don't know, maybe got an 8, 8 or a 9x and then there was some extra, an extra portion that was valued for the SaaS bit of it.
But yeah, it wasn't really a pure play SaaS.

But I do, I do advocate for this quite a lot with our clients or people that are making queries about whether it's time to sell is if they can build a piece of SaaS in front of a service that you can really like, multiply the value in a huge way.
Yeah, it will really change the valuation.
And then on the buy side, you know, the prices get pushed up just based on really good management, really good clients, really good work, reputation, etc.
Etc.
Long contracts, if you have people in contracts versus lots of project work, you know, it changes what that multiple can look like.
So I would say that there's like this sort of base rate that's somewhere around a 4 or a 5 and then you cannot keep adding 1 x's onto that based on some other factors.
Okay.
And you're still seeing quite a lot of activity by the sounds of it.
From the buy side.
We're seeing tons of activity both on the buy and the sell side.
Buy.
We are particularly busy right now on the buy side.
We just bought a business ourself, which is buy side business.
So we're seeing tons more of it anyway.
But yeah, I would say that everything is really strong right now.
I think there's been some reservations waiting for Trump to come in.
A lot of our works with America.
So.
Okay.
But it was more, it was like a rubber band pinging.
As soon as he was in, everything seemed to still exist.
Then everybody was back in the game.
But that was just timing.
I think it's been busy last year and the end of last year.
We haven't really seen any slowdown.
There's always a benefit to somebody depending on what the market looks like and.
Is that activity then a lot of US organizations coming across and acquiring in the UK or.
Well, I would say 95% of what we're doing is with the US in one way or another.
But we did have an Israeli client as well that we sold into a US group.

So I would say generally speaking it's very strong economy in the US and they are looking to get footholds in the UK and the EU sort of generally Also it's very cheap actually to acquire teams over here and then service the business in the us.
So you know, wavies are very sort of suppressed in the in the UK versus the US you know, hiring somebody in California like 150 grand for somebody who's just at a university doing a marketing role.
So you know it's, it's attractive to acquire stuff to service and we are well known the British for our creativity and the quality of the work we do versus versus the Yanks.
So they're happy to come over here and pick us up.
Yeah, I would say that was a big key part of what we would be looking to do is try and find an American buyer.
And so from that sell side process, what is your.
I know Brian's probably talked this through with you already so apologies but what is that sell side process?
And yeah, so we shoot for a sort of six month window start to finish.
The first month is really set up.

What we're looking to do is create all the marketing materials and do that valuation of the business so we're confident where we're pitching it and then once we're ready to go to market, so that's creating a SIM CIM or an IM people call lots of different things.
Basically it's a pitch deck for bankers.
And then we get your listing set up on agencies as well and then we're putting together things like teasers, et cetera.
So all of that set up is in the first month and we build a list of likely targets as well.
So not only do we go out to our agencies, co platform subscribers, there's 20,000 subscribers to our mailing list on there.
So those are active buyers.
We also have a CRM of about 130,000 plus agencies as well.
So we're looking for sort of keyword searches in our own CRM as well to find other likely matches.
And then our analysts also go out, they have a look at the latest news and they see who's bought what recently.
And he was really active and we're sort of building sort of Three layers of targeting that we go out to market with.
It's anonymized at that point, so, you know, you're not needing.
It's completely anonymous.
Yeah.
Nobody knows who you are.
At the point where the NDA is signed on our agency's platform, that triggers an automation.

And part of that is you see who the buyer potentially is, and if you don't like them or, you know, them or whatever fear you have around it and you want to reject it, then they don't get to see who the seller is.
It's only if you've approved it.
And then we release the IM then to the potential buyer and then we will answer any initial questions.
Sometimes we have to have a couple of meetings with them ourselves and then we book them in your calendar for a chemistry test, basically.
And if you like them, then we can move forward with, start releasing more details.
If you don't, you know, there's no chance that you would sell to them, then we just up the drawbridge and don't speak to them anymore.
So that usually starts happening around weeks five and six.
And then I would say there's about two or three pretty solid months of us, you know, really pushing it out to everybody that we can find and getting as many meetings for you as possible.
And then by the end of about three or four months, we usually have somebody who's really keen and an offer is very close, then we can set a deadline against all the other interested parties.
And then we're looking to get sort of three or four offers on the table.
And then it takes another two or three months to do due diligence and get the contract signed.
And that's a very general sort of timeline.
It could be.
We had a performance marketing agency that we sold in LA, we put up for sale, and we had 45 signed NDAs in the first 24 hours.
So we knew we were definitely going to find a buyer.
And I think the business was done and sold within three months.
So it really does depend sometimes, you know, it just is natural fit for somebody or for a lot of people.
And it's easy, you know, to get.
To get the deal done.
I say relatively easy, but, you know, still a lot of work.
And your fees, how does your structure work?
Yes, there's a couple of ways of doing it.
It's actually completely free to list on agencies co.
So if you wanted to do it yourself, you can list on there.

We take 5% on the deal, but we still swoop in as an M and A team as soon as there's any interest, then the sort of cheapest level to go in at that is five grand to get the valuation done and put all the marketing materials together and then that goes up onto the agency's platform and we put it out to our mailing list or it's 25, 24K and that could be broken up into smaller payments, but it's 24k for us to basically run the six month process and that's sort of the guaranteed way to get it out the door.
We're building all the marketing materials for you as part of it.

But also that's our team working on that, you know, five days a week for six months and if it runs over that, we keep going until we get a deal done and still the 5% at the end and it's 5% but it's netted against any retainer you paid.
So that 24k comes back out of the total.
So it just takes the risk off my team so they can dedicate the work to get it done.
But it's horses for courses.
So whatever is the sort of least riskiest or most attractive to each type of client.
You know what we find is the large clients just go for the 24k because it just makes sense they want to get it done.
Also people are just wanting to get a deal done.
It's kind of the surest way to do it.
But if it's a suck it and see, you just want to put a toe in the water, see if there's any interest.
Like I say, we got 45 signed NDAs in 24 hours and that client didn't pay a single penny to us until we closed the deal.
So, so there's lots of different ways to, to do it.
Okay, thank you.
Yeah, I can put all that in a, in an email to you guys and then you've got everything in front of you to discuss.
Useful to have an email.
I mean, I don't know how much Brian share but you clearly, from a board perspective, Brian I are the only two non execs but the, the chief exec of course is ultimately the decision maker.
So we, we need to have those conversations and make sure we're approaching at the right focus.
So if you can, if you can follow up an email, that's great, then we'll leave it with us and we'll explore it from there.
Yep, no problem with that at all.
Like I said, those three different tiers, there's something for everybody.
So depending on what you're looking to do over the next six months or so should guide that decision.
Okay.
Any other questions?
Are we good?
Not for me, Brian.
Yeah, questions.
So, all good?
All right.
Okay.
Perfect.
All right.
Fantastic.
Nice to meet you, Richard.
You, too.
Cheers.
Brian, you've got two minutes.
Yes.
Yeah.
Cheers.
All right.
See you.
Let me.

You can't remove this.
Persistent.

Brian.

summary.overview: The Business Development and M&A Strategy Discussion meeting focused on the current state and future plans for QueryClick and Corvidae, highlighted by Brian's overview of the companies' operations and revenue strategies. The conversation included insights from Andrew on the M&A market, emphasizing that while small businesses are appealing to buyers, the performance marketing sector is particularly hot for bolt-on acquisitions, with typical EBITDA multiples ranging from 4-6x. Additionally, the meeting addressed the ongoing high activity in M&A transactions, especially involving U.S. companies seeking to expand into the UK and EU markets, where British agencies are valued for their creativity and lower labor costs. The M&A process was detailed, illustrating key phases from initial valuation to contract signing, along with a breakdown of available fee structures for potential clients. Action items were assigned, including sending comprehensive fee information and strategizing the approach with the CEO.
